title: Building towers and bridges
keyIdea: Shapes with flat faces (cubes, cuboids, cylinders standing up) stack; a ball (sphere) rolls off and a cone has a point, so it can only go on top. A tower is steadier with the biggest, widest block at the bottom and each block lined up over the one below; a block tips off when its middle goes past the edge. A bridge needs two pillars the same height and a plank longer than the gap, so each end rests on a pillar; to let a toy car under, the pillars must be taller than the car.

kid: Some shapes stack. A cube has flat sides. A box has flat sides. Put a flat side on a flat side and it stays.
A ball is round all over. Put it on a block and it rolls off. A cone has a point on top. Nothing can sit on a point. So a cone goes last, right at the top.
Put the big block at the bottom and the small one at the top. Big on small will tip. Line each block up on the one below. If it hangs too far over the edge, it falls.
A bridge needs two posts and a long flat block on top. The block must be longer than the gap, so each end sits on a post. Make the posts the same, and taller than your car.
adult: This is early geometry and measures. Development Matters asks children of three and four to talk about 2D and 3D shapes using words such as flat, round, straight, sides and corners. They select shapes for a job, like flat surfaces for building and a prism for a roof. They combine shapes to make new ones, such as an arch, and compare objects by size and length. Positional words such as on top, under, between and next to belong here too.

The maths under the play: a face is a flat surface, a curved surface rolls, and a sphere has no flat face at all. A tower stays up while the middle of each block (its centre of mass) is over the block below. A wide base gives more room for that, which is why wide-bottomed towers are steadier. A bridge plank must span the gap and overlap both supports.

Common mistakes: trying to balance a ball or put a cone in the middle; starting with a small block and putting the big one on top; pushing blocks off-centre until the tower tips; choosing a plank that is just as long as the gap, so it falls in; and building pillars of different heights, so the plank slopes.

In the lab your child drags shapes onto a tower to see which ones stay, builds big-to-small towers, slides a block until its middle is over the one below, picks a plank long enough to make a bridge, and adds blocks to the pillars until a car and a bus can drive under.

familyTip: Build with real blocks, boxes or tins. Before each block goes on, ask: will it stay? Then make a bridge for a toy car and ask how many blocks the posts need.

visual.caption: Good at the bottom of a tower? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

bins: 🧱 Flat faces: good at the bottom
⚽ Round or pointy: not at the bottom

lab.caption: Flagship lab: stack shapes and see which stay, build big-to-small towers, line blocks up, pick a plank for a bridge, and make the pillars tall enough for a car.

practice.prompt: Which one will stay on top of a tower?
practice.hint: Which one has a flat face to sit on?
practice.explain: A cube has flat faces, so it sits still. A ball and an egg are round, so they roll off.

practice.prompt: Your tower is {n} blocks tall. You put 1 more block on top. How tall is it now?
practice.explain: {n} and 1 more is {=n+1}, so the tower is {=n+1} blocks tall.

practice.prompt: You have a big block and a small block. Which goes at the bottom?
practice.hint: Think about big on small. Will it tip?
practice.explain: The big block goes at the bottom. A wide bottom is steady. Big on small can tip over.

practice.prompt: A bridge has 2 posts. Each post is {n} blocks tall. Then 1 long block goes on top. How many blocks is that?
practice.hint: Count the blocks in both posts, then add the long one.
practice.explain: Two posts of {n} make {=2*n}, and the long block on top makes {=2*n+1}.

pool.prompt: Why does a ball roll off a tower?
pool.hint: Look at the outside of a ball. Is any part flat?
pool.explain: A ball has no flat face. It is round all over, so it rolls off.

pool.prompt: Where can a cone go on a tower?
pool.hint: Can a block sit on a point?
pool.explain: A cone has a point on top, so nothing can sit on it. It can only be the top.

pool.prompt: A block hangs far over the edge of the one below. What happens?
pool.hint: Is the middle of the block still over the block below?
pool.explain: If its middle goes past the edge, it tips off. Line it up over the block below.

pool.prompt: The gap is 3 blocks wide. Which plank makes a bridge?
pool.hint: Each end must sit on a post.
pool.explain: 4 is longer than the gap, so both ends rest on a post. 3 just fits the gap, so it falls in.

pool.prompt: One post is 3 blocks tall. The other is 1 block tall. What happens to the plank?
choices: It slopes and can slide off
pool.hint: Are the posts the same height?
pool.explain: The posts are not the same, so the plank slopes. Make both posts the same height.

pool.prompt: The gap is {g} blocks wide. What is the shortest plank, in whole blocks, that rests on both posts?
pool.hint: Just as long as the gap falls in. It must be longer.
pool.explain: A plank of {g} falls in. One more block, {=g+1}, is longer than the gap, so each end can rest on a post.

pool.prompt: A toy car is a bit taller than {n} blocks. How many blocks tall must each post be to let it under?
pool.hint: The posts must be taller than the car.
pool.explain: {n} blocks is too low, so each post needs {=n+1} blocks.

pool.prompt: Which tower is the most steady?
choices: Wide at the bottom, thin at the top
Thin at the bottom, wide at the top
All the blocks pushed to one side
pool.hint: Which one has the big block at the bottom?
pool.explain: A wide bottom is steady. Thin at the bottom, or pushed to one side, will tip.
